task.name: Test processes a dev agent spawns outlive the sprint that started them and go on consuming the host indefinitely
task.story_text:
## Observed

Test processes a dev agent spawns inside its sandbox outlive the sprint that created them, and go
on consuming the machine indefinitely.

Story `issue-2284`'s dev agent ran the project's own suite four times while working, three of them
with `pytest -n auto --dist worksteal`, concurrently. Those invocations never terminated. Thirteen
hours after the sprint completed and its worktree was deleted, the machine still carried:

```
40 processes, ~321% CPU total
parent 4129   13:20:23  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py::...
parent 68119  13:56:07  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 71222  13:51:50  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 85040  13:41:11  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q
```

The parents were alive, not orphaned children of a reaped tree, and every worker executed from
`.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv` — a path that no longer exists, held open by the running
processes.

The effect was not confined to wasted CPU. Every gate run on this host afterwards competed with
roughly three cores of dead test workers: a `make gate` that normally completes in about 55
seconds took 181, and a wall-clock timeout test failed inside it while passing three times out of
three when run alone. That failure was read as a possible regression in an unrelated story. Every
run duration recorded during those thirteen hours — the same durations adaptive limits derive dev
timeouts from — was measured against a host under load that nothing accounted for.

## Expected

Work a sprint starts should not outlive the sprint. A story's agent runs inside a sandbox with a
worktree, a virtualenv and a budget, all of which end when the story does; a process it spawned is
part of that same envelope and should end with it, whether the story succeeded, failed, or was
stopped.

The failure is quiet in a way that matters. A leaked process produces no artifact, no cost record
and no log line, so nothing in the run reports it and nothing in a later run knows it is there.
What it changes instead is every timing measurement taken afterwards on the same host — which is
the input the system uses to decide how long work should be allowed to take. A leak that only
wasted CPU would be a nuisance; one that silently biases the measurements the scheduler learns
from is a correctness problem for everything measured while it persists.

That an agent runs the suite at all is reasonable and worth keeping. That it can run it several
times concurrently, each fanning out across every core, inside an environment already running
under the coordinator's own parallelism, is a resource decision nobody made — the agent has no way
to know what else is executing, so the bound has to come from the side that does.

## Diagnosis

- **Observed symptom:** pytest processes spawned by a dev agent remain running and consuming CPU
  long after the sprint that started them has completed and its worktree has been removed.
- **Evidence:** four `pytest` parents with elapsed times of 13h20m–13h56m, PPIDs alive, and 40
  associated workers totalling ~321% CPU, all executing `.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv/bin/python`
  after that worktree was deleted. Three carried `-n auto --dist worksteal`. The sprint that
  spawned them had completed and landed via #2285.
- **Ruled out:** not the 21-day-old orphaned `codex exec` pair from another project — those are
  idle, 13 minutes of CPU across 21 days, and unrelated.
- **Ruled out:** not a worktree-cleanup failure. The worktree was removed; the processes held the
  freed inode open, which is why they remained visible under a path that no longer resolves.
- **Confirmed cause:** processes started by an agent inside its sandbox are not part of anything
  the sprint tears down at story end, so a subprocess that does not exit on its own persists
  without limit.
- **Affected code path:** sandbox process supervision and story teardown.
- **Fix-success criterion:** a process a story's agent starts does not outlive the story, whatever
  the story's outcome, and a process that has to be terminated at teardown is recorded so the run
  shows it happened. The suite remains runnable by an agent; what it cannot do is leave work
  behind.

handoff.summary: Fixed both P1s and both P2s from cycle 1. P1 (reaper): a stopped sprint could not reap a descendant that had left its process group and whose environment cannot be read — the live path covers that case by observing the descendant while its parent link still existed, but the observation died with the sprint. DescendantTracker now takes an on_observed callback, and process_group.record_observed_descendants persists each new observation into the group's sidecar as it is made; reap_orphan_agents passes that snapshot to kill_escapees, which verifies every pid against the start time it was recorded with before signalling, so a recycled id is left alone (#2115). A single descendant_tracker() factory now builds the trackers at all three spawn sites so none can register a group and watch it without leaving the durable record. P1 (gate ordinal): the teardown append ran before _record_gate_run, filing the first gate's leak under gate_run 0; it now runs after, through one _record_gate_teardowns recorder that drains the collector — which also let the gate-debug and gate-diagnostic shells (previously passing no teardown_out at all, per the reviewer's coverage note) record their own leaks against the gate that ran. P2: group_members returned {} both for an empty group and for a failed read, so a sysctl returning nothing under load looked like a settled group and dropped a live group's record without a kill; group_members_checked now reports whether the enumeration completed and only a completed one may overrule the liveness probe. Also re-added tests/test_process_tree.py, which the rebase dropped and which is a blocking mirror violation.

Extended beyond the two cited lines to the same defect's other sites, per the pattern-bug instruction: the gate ordinal fix covers gate-debug and gate-diagnostic as well as the main gate, and the enumeration fix covers both the darwin and linux readers plus the b-empty-vs-None conflation on the sysctl path.

handoff.summary: Advisory cleanup after APPROVE, addressing all three carried P2s without redesigning anything. (1) dev_verification.py: VerificationRequestExecutor._execute now passes a teardown_out collector to _run_shell_detailed, and VerificationRequestRecord gained a process_teardown field emitted conditionally from audit_payload() — a declared verification command is usually a build or test run executed outside the dev sandbox, so it is the same leak shape as the gate, and the kill it already received is now visible in the run's record. (2) sprint/runner.py: _run_baseline_gate passes a process_teardowns collector to run_gate_full and includes the teardowns in the baseline record it returns on both the pass and the fail path; the baseline gate runs the project's gate command before any story exists to own the record. (3) process_group.kill_escapees: corrected a docstring that claimed every target is identity-checked against a recorded start time. That is not what the code does and should not be — a pid is not identity so both observation signals re-check it, but a lease token is identity (minted once per spawn, never reused) so there is nothing older to check it against, and the start time read on that path exists only to give wait_until_gone something to compare. Also swept all five _run_shell_detailed call sites for the same gap: four now record; _run_shell's short git commands deliberately do not, since they cannot leak a test tree and have no per-call audit home.

handoff.summary: P1: pre_validate_command ran through _cu._run_shell, which dropped the teardown collector, so a project command configured to run after a passing gate had its leaked workers killed with nothing in the run record. _run_shell now threads teardown_out and the validate phase records the teardown. Because four different commands run in that phase (gate, gate-debug, gate-diagnostic, pre-validate) and all were recorded in one indistinguishable shape, entries now carry a 'source' field — a record that cannot say which command leaked sends an operator to the wrong trace. That is a pinned-list shape change, so CURRENT_RECORD_SCHEMA_VERSION goes 24 -> 25 with _migrate_v24_to_v25 backfilling source='gate' (correct rather than null: v24 only ever collected from the gate-family shells) and a regenerated v25 snapshot. P2 (third appearance of the kill_escapees family): I did not apply the suggested short-circuit — skipping the sweep when the group is empty and no tracker survivors exist would skip exactly the escapee the lease exists for, since a setsid escapee leaves an empty group and, if born between two samples, was never observed. The actual defect was how much the sweep reads: every process's environment on every shell release, measured at 15.3ms of a 16.1ms /usr/bin/true. The candidate set is now bounded by a sound fact rather than a guess — a descendant cannot predate its ancestor — so one KERN_PROC_ALL sysctl yields the whole table's start times and KERN_PROCARGS2 is read only for what survives the filter. Measured: 625 processes prune to 2 in 0.25ms; overhead over raw subprocess.run is 0.51ms, down from ~14ms. Verified the prune still finds a real leaked descendant, that kinfo start times agree with libproc's independent read to the microsecond, and that the reaper's undated sweep (started_at=0.0) still considers the whole table.

story_deviations: The P2 was not fixed as suggested. Short-circuiting kill_escapees when the group is empty and the tracker recorded no survivors would skip the escapee case the lease layer exists for; the cost was addressed by bounding the candidate set on a sound invariant instead. Stated explicitly because the divergence from the reviewer's proposed fix is deliberate.

The lease-sweep prune is applied on macOS only. Linux reads a small pseudo-file per process rather than copying an argv+environ blob, so its scan is already sub-millisecond, and the /proc/<pid> ctime the filter would need could not be verified on the platform this branch was developed on. A prune that is wrong does not run slowly — it silently stops finding leaks.

Wider than this finding warrants; the teardown still happens and is logged. Every other _run_shell caller is a short git query.

findings.description: When a sprint is stopped after an agent starts a detached platform-binary subprocess, the later orphan sweep can report zero reaped processes and leave that subprocess running after discarding the story sidecar.
When the first validation gate leaks a worker, the audit entry records gate_run as 0 while the run counter later records that one gate ran.

Gate teardowns are recorded against the pre-increment gate_runs counter because the append happens before _record_gate_run, so the first leak in a run is tagged gate_run 0 while every other run-gated telemetry begins at 1.
On a platform where group_members cannot enumerate (sysctl/kinfo read failure), a group that is alive but reports empty members is treated as gone and its sidecar is dropped without any kill.

findings.description: The reaper's kill_escapees applies the start-time identity check to tracker survivors, recorded observations and lease holders, but the live release path (release_group_record) passes a tracker whose survivors() already re-checked identity, while lease holders found on the live path are recorded with a fresh fingerprint read at kill time — so the identity discipline documented as applying to every target is not uniformly exercised on the live path's lease matches.

A dev verification command (VerificationRequestExecutor._execute) runs through _run_shell_detailed without a teardown_out collector, so when one of these commands leaves processes that release_group_record has to kill, the forced teardown is logged but not recorded in any run audit field.

The sprint-level baseline gate calls run_gate_full without a process_teardowns collector, so a baseline gate that leaks workers (killed at release) is not represented in any per-run gate_process_teardowns record.

ac_verification.criterion: A process a story's agent starts does not outlive the story, whatever the story's outcome.
ac_verification.evidence: Runtime containment is invoked from the runner and gate spawn paths: src/theforge/process_group.py:334 opens a per-spawn lease, src/theforge/process_group.py:354 starts the durable descendant tracker, src/theforge/process_group.py:377 releases the group with lease and tracker, src/theforge/coordinator/util.py:403 and src/theforge/coordinator/util.py:438 apply the same machinery to gate shells, and src/theforge/runners/runner_claude.py:819 through src/theforge/runners/runner_claude.py:935 wires Claude through registration, tracking, and release. finding_registry.description: When a sprint is stopped after an agent starts a detached platform-binary subprocess, the later orphan sweep can report zero reaped processes and leave that subprocess running after discarding the story sidecar.
When the first validation gate leaks a worker, the audit entry records gate_run as 0 while the run counter later records that one gate ran.

Gate teardowns are recorded against the pre-increment gate_runs counter because the append happens before _record_gate_run, so the first leak in a run is tagged gate_run 0 while every other run-gated telemetry begins at 1.
On a platform where group_members cannot enumerate (sysctl/kinfo read failure), a group that is alive but reports empty members is treated as gone and its sidecar is dropped without any kill.

The reaper's kill_escapees applies the start-time identity check to tracker survivors, recorded observations and lease holders, but the live release path (release_group_record) passes a tracker whose survivors() already re-checked identity, while lease holders found on the live path are recorded with a fresh fingerprint read at kill time — so the identity discipline documented as applying to every target is not uniformly exercised on the live path's lease matches.

A dev verification command (VerificationRequestExecutor._execute) runs through _run_shell_detailed without a teardown_out collector, so when one of these commands leaves processes that release_group_record has to kill, the forced teardown is logged but not recorded in any run audit field.

The sprint-level baseline gate calls run_gate_full without a process_teardowns collector, so a baseline gate that leaks workers (killed at release) is not represented in any per-run gate_process_teardowns record.

The pre-validate command (config.validation.pre_validate_command) runs through _cu._run_shell, which suppresses the teardown collector, so a pre-validate command that spawns long-lived test workers gets them killed at release but the run's audit record never shows the kill happened.

Every _run_shell_detailed call now opens a process lease and release_group_record always invokes kill_escapees, which calls lease_holders and scans the whole process table reading each process's environment, even when a short command left nothing behind.

When a v24 audit record contains a validation teardown produced by the gate debug or diagnostic shell, the reader-side migration reports that teardown with source gate, so the migrated record points at the main gate even though the older record did not identify which validation shell leaked.

When a v24 audit record contains a teardown from the gate-debug or gate-diagnostic shell, reading it through _migrate_v24_to_v25 rewrites its source to 'gate', so the audit record sends an operator to the main gate trace instead of the command that actually leaked.

ProcessTeardown.pgid is typed int | None and to_audit_dict serializes None when a spawn's group cannot be resolved, but the pinned audit schema (tests/fixtures/audit_record_schema_v25.json) declares cost.agents[].process_teardown.pgid as int.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
